title: Design a class that, given a value K and an initial list of numbers, returns the Kth largest number each time a new number is added to the stream. Explain how a min-heap of size K supports this efficiently.
shortTitle: Kth Largest Number in a Stream (Maintain the Kth Largest as Numbers Arrive)

s1_definition.profdef: Kth Largest Number in a Stream is a Top K Elements design problem. We maintain a min-heap bounded to size K containing the K largest numbers seen so far. The root of this heap is always the Kth largest. When a new number arrives we offer it and, if the heap exceeds K, poll the root, so the root remains the Kth largest and each add is O(log K).
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, we continuously watch incoming transaction amounts and must always report the Kth largest so far, for a live threshold alert. We keep a small bucket of the K largest amounts with the smallest of those K on top; that top value is the Kth largest, and each new amount updates it cheaply.
s1_definition.oneliner: Keep a min-heap of size K of the largest numbers; its root is always the Kth largest as the stream grows.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Kth Largest Number in a Stream is a Top K Elements design problem. We maintain a min-heap bounded to size K containing the K largest numbers seen so far. The root of this heap is always the Kth largest. When a new number arrives we offer it and, if the heap exceeds K, poll the root, so the root remains the Kth largest and each add is O(log K).

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, we continuously watch incoming transaction amounts and must always report the Kth largest so far, for a live threshold alert. We keep a small bucket of the K largest amounts with the smallest of those K on top; that top value is the Kth largest, and each new amount updates it cheaply.

**One line to remember:** Keep a min-heap of size K of the largest numbers; its root is always the Kth largest as the stream grows.

sections.s2_technical:
The class holds a min-heap and the value K. In the constructor we add all initial numbers via the same add routine so the heap self-limits to K. The `add(num)` method offers the number and, if `minHeap.size() > k`, polls the root: `minHeap.offer(num); if (minHeap.size() > k) minHeap.poll(); return minHeap.peek();`. The peek returns the current Kth largest.

Keeping the heap at exactly K elements means the smallest of the K largest, the root, is by definition the Kth largest overall. Adding a number that is too small to be in the top K will be immediately polled back out, so it never disturbs the answer; adding a number large enough pushes the old Kth largest out and the new root becomes the updated Kth largest.

A senior nuance is that this is a stateful streaming design, so correctness depends on always re-trimming to K after each insert, and on seeding the heap through the same add path to avoid duplicated logic. Each add is O(log K) and the structure uses O(K) space regardless of how long the stream runs, which is the key scalability property. Complexity is O(log K) per add and O(K) space.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India runs a live threshold alert that must always know the Kth largest transaction amount seen so far on a never-ending stream, to flag unusually large activity. This is exactly how Kth Largest in a Stream works.

Problem 2 — Storing and re-sorting the whole stream is impossible as it grows without bound. This is why we keep only a size-K min-heap whose root is the Kth largest, using fixed memory no matter how long the stream runs.

The code defines a `KthLargestStream` class with `add(amount)` returning the current Kth largest. A `Demo` seeds it and feeds several amounts, logging the Kth largest after each.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: K equal to 3, initial amounts 4000, 1000, 8000, 3000, then adds 5000, 2000, 9000.

Step 1: Seeding adds 4000, 1000, 8000 to fill the heap. Adding 3000 makes size four, so poll the smallest, 1000; the heap holds 3000, 4000, 8000 with root 3000, the Kth largest.

Step 2: Add 5000; size becomes four, poll smallest 3000; the heap holds 4000, 5000, 8000 with root 4000, so the Kth largest is 4000.

Step 3: Add 2000; size becomes four, poll smallest 2000 immediately since it is the new smallest; the heap stays 4000, 5000, 8000 with root 4000, so the Kth largest is still 4000.

Step 4: Add 9000; size becomes four, poll smallest 4000; the heap holds 5000, 8000, 9000 with root 5000, so the Kth largest is 5000.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Kth Largest Number in a Stream is a stateful design problem from the Top K Elements family. The structure I maintain is a min-heap bounded to size K that always contains the K largest numbers seen so far. Because it is a min-heap, its root is the smallest of those K, which is exactly the Kth largest overall, so answering a query is just reading the root.

When a new number arrives I offer it into the heap and then, if the heap now holds more than K elements, I poll the root to trim it back to K. A number too small to belong in the top K gets polled straight back out and never affects the answer, while a large enough number pushes the old Kth largest out and the new root becomes the updated Kth largest. I also seed the initial numbers through the very same add routine so there is only one place that enforces the size limit.

At the National Bank of India I used this for a live threshold alert that had to always know the Kth largest transaction amount on a never-ending stream, flagging unusually large activity. Keeping only a size-K min-heap meant fixed memory no matter how long the stream ran, with each update costing just the logarithm of K. Explaining why the root of a size-K min-heap is the Kth largest, and why the memory stays constant for an unbounded stream, is what shows an interviewer I can design for streaming, not just batch.
